Chapter 7 · Geography · Contemporary India II

Lifelines of National Economy

Goods and services do not move by themselves. This chapter explains why transport, communication and trade are called the lifelines of a nation: the six classes of roads, the 17 railway zones, national waterways, twelve major ports, UDAN, the postal and telecom network, balance of trade and tourism.

Chapter Overview

What this chapter is about, at a glance

We use different materials and services in our daily life. Some are available in our immediate surroundings, while other requirements are met by bringing things from other places. Goods and services do not move from supply locales to demand locales on their own. The movement of goods and services necessitates the need for transport, and some people — traders — facilitate these movements. Thus the pace of development of a country depends upon the production of goods and services as well as their movement over space. Efficient means of transport are prerequisites for fast development.

Movement can be over three important domains of our earth — land, water and air — so transport is classified into land, water and air transport. Transport needs an equally developed communication system, and transport, communication and trade are complementary to each other.

The chapter works through each mode: roadways (six classes, including the Golden Quadrilateral and border roads), railways (17 zones, gauges, the Konkan Railway), pipelines, waterways (five national waterways) and sea ports, then airways and communication.

It ends with international trade — exports, imports and balance of trade — and tourism as a trade, with schemes such as Swadesh Darshan 2.0, PRASHAD and Paryatan Mitra.

Road network

Second largest in the world, about 62.16 lakh km (2020–21); roads preceded railways and still have an edge.

Golden Quadrilateral

Six-lane super highways linking Delhi–Kolkata–Chennai–Mumbai–Delhi, plus the North–South and East–West corridors, implemented by NHAI.

Railways

Reorganised into 17 zones; the first train ran from Mumbai to Thane in 1853 over 34 km; the network runs on 67,956 km of track.

Waterways

Inland navigation waterways of 14,500 km; 111 inland waterways declared National Waterways by the National Waterways Act, 2016.

Ports

Coastline of 11,098.81 km; 12 major and 200 notified non-major ports; sea carries 95 per cent of trade volume (68 per cent by value).

Communication

The Indian postal network is the largest in the world; India has one of the largest telecom networks in Asia.

Trade

Balance of trade = exports minus imports; favourable if exports exceed imports.

Tourism

Schemes include Swadesh Darshan 2.0, Vibrant Village Programme, PRASHAD and Paryatan Mitra.

Why Transport, Communication and Trade Matter

We use different materials and services in our daily life. Some of these are available in our immediate surroundings, while other requirements are met by bringing things from other places. Goods and services do not move from supply locales to demand locales on their own. The movement of these goods and services from their supply locations to demand locations necessitates the need for transport. Some people are engaged in facilitating these movements — these are known as traders, who make the products come to the consumers by transportation.

Thus, the pace of development of a country depends upon the production of goods and services as well as their movement over space. Therefore, efficient means of transport are prerequisites for fast development.

Movement of goods and services can be over three important domains of our earth — land, water and air. Based on these, transport can be classified into land, water and air transport.

For a long time, trade and transport were restricted to a limited space. With the development in science and technology, the area of influence of trade and transport expanded far and wide. Today, the world has been converted into a large village with the help of efficient and fast-moving transport. Transport has been able to achieve this with the help of an equally developed communication system. Therefore, transport, communication and trade are complementary to each other.

Today, India is well linked with the rest of the world despite its vast size, diversity and linguistic and socio-cultural plurality. Railways, airways, waterways, newspapers, radio, television, cinema and internet, etc., have been contributing to its socio-economic progress in many ways. Trade from local to international levels has added to the vitality of its economy. It has enriched our life and added substantially to growing amenities and facilities for the comforts of life.

In this chapter you will see how modern means of transport and communication serve as lifelines of our nation and its modern economy. It is thus evident that a dense and efficient network of transport and communication is a prerequisite for local, national and global trade of today.

Roadways

India has the second largest road networks in the world, aggregating to about 62.16 lakh km (2020–21). In India, roadways have preceded railways. They still have an edge over railways in view of the ease with which they can be built and maintained.

The growing importance of road transport vis-à-vis rail transport is rooted in the following reasons:

  1. Construction cost of roads is much lower than that of railway lines.
  2. Roads can traverse comparatively more dissected and undulating topography.
  3. Roads can negotiate higher gradients of slopes and as such can traverse mountains such as the Himalayas.
  4. Road transport is economical in transportation of few persons and relatively smaller amount of goods over short distances.
  5. It also provides door-to-door service, thus the cost of loading and unloading is much lower.
  6. Road transport is also used as a feeder to other modes of transport, as they provide a link between railway stations, air and sea ports.

In India, roads are classified in the following six classes according to their capacity.

Six classes of roads in India
ClassWhat it links
Golden Quadrilateral Super HighwaysDelhi–Kolkata–Chennai–Mumbai–Delhi by six-lane super highways; the North–South corridor links Srinagar (Jammu and Kashmir) and Kanniyakumari (Tamil Nadu), and the East–West corridor connects Silchar (Assam) and Porbandar (Gujarat). The major objective is to reduce the time and distance between the mega cities of India. Implemented by the National Highway Authority of India (NHAI).
National HighwaysLink extreme parts of the country; the primary road systems. A number of major National Highways run in north–south and east–west directions.
State HighwaysRoads linking a state capital with different district headquarters.
District RoadsConnect the district headquarters with other places of the district.
Other RoadsRural roads linking rural areas and villages with towns. They received special impetus under the Pradhan Mantri Grameen Sadak Yojana, under which special provisions are made so that every village is linked to a major town by an all-season motorable road.
Border RoadsConstructed and maintained by the Border Roads Organisation, a Government of India undertaking, in the bordering areas. Established in 1960 for the development of roads of strategic importance in the northern and north-eastern border areas; these roads have improved accessibility in areas of difficult terrain and helped economic development.

Roads can also be classified on the basis of the type of material used for their construction, such as metalled and unmetalled roads. Metalled roads may be made of cement, concrete or even bitumen of coal, and are therefore all-weather roads. Unmetalled roads go out of use in the rainy season.

Box: Atal Tunnel

The world’s longest highway tunnel — Atal Tunnel (9.02 km) — has been built by the Border Roads Organisation. This tunnel connects Manali to the Lahul-Spiti valley throughout the year. Earlier the valley was cut off for about six months each year owing to heavy snowfall. The tunnel is built with ultra-modern specifications in the Pir Panjal range of the Himalayas at an altitude of 3,000 metres from the mean sea level.

Collect information on National Highway numbers (old and new) from the website morth.nic.in. The historical Sher Shah Suri Marg between Delhi and Amritsar is known by which National Highway?

Railways

Railways are the principal mode of transportation for freight and passengers in India. Railways also make it possible for people to conduct multifarious activities like business, sightseeing and pilgrimage along with transportation of goods over longer distances. Apart from being an important means of transport, the Indian Railways have been a great integrating force for more than 150 years. Railways in India bind the economic life of the country as well as accelerate the development of industry and agriculture.

The Indian Railways is the largest public sector undertaking in the country. The first train steamed off from Mumbai to Thane in 1853, covering a distance of 34 km. The Indian Railway is now reorganised into 17 zones.

The distribution pattern of the railway network in the country has been largely influenced by physiographic, economic and administrative factors.

  • The northern plains with their vast level land, high population density and rich agricultural resources provided the most favourable conditions for their growth. However, a large number of rivers requiring construction of bridges across their wide beds posed some obstacles.
  • In the hilly terrains of the peninsular region, railway tracks are laid through low hills, gaps or tunnels.
  • The Himalayan mountainous regions are unfavourable for the construction of railway lines due to high relief, sparse population and lack of economic opportunities.
  • It was difficult to lay railway lines on the sandy plain of western Rajasthan, swamps of Gujarat, and forested tracks of Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Odisha and Jharkhand.
  • The contiguous stretch of Sahyadri could be crossed only through gaps or passes (ghats). In recent times, the development of the Konkan Railway along the west coast has facilitated the movement of passengers and goods in this most important economic region of India. It has also faced a number of problems such as sinking of track in some stretches and landslides.

Today the railways have become more important in our national economy than all other means of transport put together. However, rail transport suffers from certain problems as well. Many passengers travel without tickets. Thefts and damaging of railway property have not yet stopped completely. People stop the trains, pull the chain unnecessarily and this causes heavy damage to the railway.

Pipelines

Pipeline transport network is a new arrival on the transportation map of India. In the past these were used to transport water to cities and industries. Now these are used for transporting crude oil, petroleum products and natural gas from oil and natural gas fields to refineries, fertiliser factories and big thermal power plants. Solids can also be transported through a pipeline when converted into slurry.

The far inland locations of refineries like Barauni, Mathura and Panipat and gas-based fertiliser plants could be thought of only because of pipelines. Initial cost of laying pipelines is high but subsequent running costs are minimal. It rules out trans-shipment losses or delays.

There are three important networks of pipeline transportation in the country:

  1. From oil fields in upper Assam to Kanpur (Uttar Pradesh), via Guwahati, Barauni and Prayagraj. It has branches from Barauni to Haldia via Rajbandh, Rajbandh to Maurigram and Guwahati to Siliguri.
  2. From Salaya in Gujarat to Jalandhar in Punjab, via Viramgam, Mathura, Delhi and Sonipat. It has branches to connect Koyali (near Vadodara, Gujarat), Chakshu and other places.
  3. The first 1,700 km long Hazira–Vijaipur–Jagdishpur (HVJ) cross-country gas pipeline, which linked Mumbai High and Bassein gas fields with various fertiliser, power and industrial complexes in western and northern India. Overall, India’s gas pipeline infrastructure has expanded from 1,700 km to 18,500 km of cross-country pipelines.
Waterways

Since the ancient period, India was one of the seafaring countries. Its seamen sailed far and near, thus carrying and spreading Indian commerce and culture. Waterways are the cheapest means of transport. They are most suitable for carrying heavy and bulky goods. It is a fuel-efficient and environment-friendly mode of transport.

India has inland navigation waterways of 14,500 km in length. In order to create a wide waterways network and to promote inland water transport as an economical, environment-friendly supplementary mode of transport to rail and road, 111 inland waterways (including 5 National Waterways declared earlier) were declared as National Waterways (NWs) by the National Waterways Act, 2016.

The five National Waterways described in the chapter
WaterwayStretchLength
N.W. No. 1The Ganga river between Prayagraj and Haldia1,620 km
N.W. No. 2The Brahmaputra river between Sadiya and Dhubri891 km
N.W. No. 3The West-Coast Canal in Kerala (Kottapurma–Kollam, Udyogamandal and Champakkara canals)205 km
N.W. No. 4Specified stretches of the Godavari and Krishna rivers along with the Kakinada–Puducherry stretch of canals1,078 km
N.W. No. 5Specified stretches of the river Brahmani along with the Matai river, delta channels of the Mahanadi and Brahmani rivers and the East Coast Canal588 km

There are some other inland waterways on which substantial transportation takes place: Mandavi, Zuari and Cumberjua, Sunderbans, Barak and the backwaters of Kerala.

Apart from these, India’s trade with foreign countries is carried from the ports located along the coast. 95 per cent of the country’s trade volume (68 per cent in terms of value) is moved by sea.

Major Sea Ports

With a long coastline of 11,098.81 km, India is dotted with 12 major and 200 notified non-majors (minor/intermediate) ports. These major ports handle 95 per cent of India’s foreign trade.

India’s major ports and what each is known for
PortSpecial feature
Deendayal Port (Kandla), KuchchhThe first port developed soon after Independence to ease the volume of trade on the Mumbai port, in the wake of the loss of Karachi port to Pakistan after Partition. It is a tidal port, catering to exports and imports of the granary and industrial belt stretching across UT of Jammu and Kashmir and the states of Himachal Pradesh, Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan and Gujarat.
MumbaiThe biggest port, with a spacious natural and well-sheltered harbour.
Jawaharlal Nehru PortPlanned with a view to decongest the Mumbai port and serve as a hub port for this region.
Mormugao (Goa)The premier iron ore exporting port of the country, accounting for about fifty per cent of India’s iron ore export.
New Mangalore (Karnataka)Caters to the export of iron ore concentrates from Kudremukh mines.
CochinThe extreme south-western port, located at the entrance of a lagoon with a natural harbour.
V.O. Chidambaranar (Tuticorin), Tamil NaduThe extreme south-eastern port; has a natural harbour and rich hinterland, hence flourishing trade handling a large variety of cargoes to even neighbouring countries like Sri Lanka and Maldives and the coastal regions of India.
ChennaiOne of the oldest artificial ports of the country; ranked next to Mumbai in terms of volume of trade and cargo.
VishakhapatnamThe deepest landlocked and well-protected port; originally conceived as an outlet for iron ore exports.
Paradwip (Odisha)Specialises in the export of iron ore.
Shyama Prasad Mookerjee, KolkataAn inland riverine port serving a very large and rich hinterland of the Ganga–Brahmaputra basin. Being a tidal port, it requires constant dredging of the Hoogly.
HaldiaDeveloped as a subsidiary port in order to relieve growing pressure on the Kolkata port.
Airways

Air travel today is the fastest, most comfortable and prestigious mode of transport. It can cover very difficult terrains like high mountains, dreary deserts, dense forests and also long oceanic stretches with great ease.

Think of the north-eastern part of the country, marked by the presence of big rivers, dissected relief, dense forests, frequent floods and international frontiers — in the absence of air transport, access would be very difficult. Air travel has made access easier.

Pawanhans Helicopters Ltd. provides helicopter services to the Oil and Natural Gas Corporation in its off-shore operations, to inaccessible areas and difficult terrains like the north-eastern states and the interior parts of Jammu and Kashmir, Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand.

Box: UDAN

UDAN (Ude Desh ka Aam Nagrik) is a first-of-its-kind scheme globally, designed to jump-start the regional aviation market. Regional Connectivity Scheme (RCS)–UDAN was conceived by the Ministry of Civil Aviation (MoCA), Government of India, to promote regional connectivity by making flying affordable for the common citizen. The central idea of the scheme is to encourage airlines to operate flights on regional and remote routes through enabling policies and extending incentives.

Communication

Ever since humans appeared on the earth, they have used different means of communication. But the pace of change has been rapid in modern times. Long-distance communication is far easier without physical movement of the communicator or receiver.

Personal communication and mass communication including television, radio, press, films, etc., are the major means of communication in the country.

The Indian postal network is the largest in the world. It handles parcels as well as personal written communications. Cards and envelopes are considered first-class mail and are airlifted between stations covering both land and air. The second-class mail includes book packets, registered newspapers and periodicals; they are carried by surface mail, covering land and water transport.

To facilitate quick delivery of mails in large towns and cities, six mail channels have been introduced recently: Rajdhani Channel, Metro Channel, Green Channel, Business Channel, Bulk Mail Channel and Periodical Channel.

India has one of the largest telecom networks in Asia. Excluding urban places, more than two-thirds of the villages in India have already been covered with Subscriber Trunk Dialling (STD) telephone facility. In order to strengthen the flow of information from the grassroot to the higher level, the government has made special provision to extend twenty-four hours STD facility to every village in the country. There is a uniform rate of STD facilities all over India. It has been made possible by integrating the development in space technology with communication technology.

Mass communication provides entertainment and creates awareness among people about various national programmes and policies. It includes radio, television, newspapers, magazines, books and films. All India Radio (Akashwani) broadcasts a variety of programmes in national, regional and local languages for various categories of people, spread over different parts of the country. Doordarshan, the national television channel of India, is one of the largest terrestrial networks in the world; it broadcasts a variety of programmes from entertainment and educational to sports for people of different age groups.

India publishes a large number of newspapers and periodicals annually. They are of different types depending upon their periodicity. Newspapers are published in about 100 languages and dialects. Did you know that the largest number of newspapers published in the country are in Hindi, followed by English and Urdu? India is the largest producer of feature films in the world. It produces short films, video feature films and video short films. The Central Board of Film Certification is the authority to certify both Indian and foreign films.

Box: Digital India

Digital India is an umbrella programme to prepare India for a knowledge-based transformation. The focus of the Digital India Programme is on being transformative, to realise — IT (Indian Talent) + IT (Information Technology) = IT (India Tomorrow) — and on making technology central to enabling change.

International Trade

The exchange of goods among people, states and countries is referred to as trade. The market is the place where such exchanges take place. Trade between two countries is called international trade. It may take place through sea, air or land routes. While local trade is carried on in cities, towns and villages, state-level trade is carried on between two or more states.

Advancement of international trade of a country is an index to its economic prosperity. It is, therefore, considered the economic barometer for a country. As the resources are space bound, no country can survive without international trade.

Export and import are the components of trade. The balance of trade of a country is the difference between its export and import. When the value of exports exceeds the value of imports, it is called a favourable balance of trade. On the contrary, if the value of imports exceeds the value of exports, it is termed an unfavourable balance of trade.

India’s exports and imports (as listed in the chapter)
Commodities exported from IndiaCommodities imported to India
Gems and jewellery, chemicals and related products, agriculture and allied products, etc.Petroleum crude and products, gems and jewellery, chemicals and related products, base metals, electronic items, machinery, agriculture and allied products

India has trade relations with all the major trading blocks and all geographical regions of the world. India has emerged as a software giant at the international level and is earning large foreign exchange through the export of information technology.

Tourism as a Trade

Tourism in India has grown remarkably over the past two decades, with government initiatives, infrastructure development and global branding contributing to this success. To boost tourism in India, schemes like Swadesh Darshan 2.0, Vibrant Village Programme, PRASHAD (Pilgrimage Rejuvenation and Spiritual Heritage Augmentation Drive) and Paryatan Mitra have been started.

Tourism also promotes national integration, provides support to local handicrafts and cultural pursuits. It also helps in the development of international understanding about our culture and heritage.

Foreign tourists visit India for heritage tourism, eco tourism, adventure tourism, cultural tourism, medical tourism and business tourism. There is a vast potential for development of tourism in all parts of the country, and efforts are being made to promote different types of tourism for this upcoming industry.

Project work

Prepare a project on heritage tourism in India. On the map of India show important tourist places of your state/UT and its connectivity with other parts of the country by railways/roadways/airways. Discuss in class: what type of tourism may be developed in your state/UT and why; which areas you find more attractive for tourism and why; and how tourism may help the economic development of a region adopting a sustainable development approach.

Activities and the Quiz Drive
Quiz Drive

Quiz Drive: (1) Northern terminal of the North–South corridor. (2) The headquarters of the Southern Railway zone. (3) The rail gauge with a track width of 1.676 m. (4) A riverine port. (5) Busiest railway junction in northern India.

Answers: (1) Srinagar (Jammu and Kashmir) — the corridor runs to Kanniyakumari. (2) Chennai. (3) Broad Gauge. (4) Shyama Prasad Mookerjee Port, Kolkata — an inland riverine port. (5) Mughalsarai (now Deen Dayal Upadhyaya junction) is the busiest junction in northern India — the chapter does not name it, so write the answer only if your teacher confirms it.

Key Terms and Definitions

Tap a card to flip it, then use the arrows to revise

Flashcards

All key terms

Key terms and definitions
TermSimple explanation
TransportThe means by which goods and services move from supply locations to demand locations; classified into land, water and air transport.
TradersPeople who make products reach consumers by transporting them from where they are produced to where they are needed.
CommunicationPersonal and mass means of exchanging information — post, telephone, radio, television, newspapers, films and the internet.
Golden QuadrilateralSix-lane super highways linking Delhi–Kolkata–Chennai–Mumbai–Delhi, plus the North–South and East–West corridors, to reduce time and distance between mega cities.
NHAIThe National Highway Authority of India, which implements the super highway projects.
National HighwaysThe primary road systems, linking extreme parts of the country, running largely north–south and east–west.
State HighwaysRoads linking a state capital with different district headquarters.
Border Roads OrganisationA Government of India undertaking, established in 1960, which constructs and maintains roads of strategic importance in the northern and north-eastern border areas.
PMGSYPradhan Mantri Grameen Sadak Yojana — under which every village is linked to a major town by an all-season motorable road.
Metalled roadA road made of cement, concrete or bitumen of coal; an all-weather road. Unmetalled roads go out of use in the rainy season.
Atal TunnelThe world’s longest highway tunnel (9.02 km), built by the Border Roads Organisation, connecting Manali to the Lahul-Spiti valley in the Pir Panjal range at 3,000 m.
GaugeThe width between railway tracks — broad gauge (1.676 m), metre gauge (1.000 m) and narrow gauge (0.762 and 0.610 m).
Konkan RailwayA railway along the west coast that has facilitated movement of passengers and goods in this important economic region, despite problems of sinking track and landslides.
Pipeline transportTransport of crude oil, petroleum products and natural gas (and solids as slurry) through pipes; high initial cost but minimal running cost, with no trans-shipment losses or delays.
SlurryA mixture of solid material with water, which allows solids to be transported through a pipeline.
National WaterwaysInland waterways declared by the National Waterways Act, 2016 — 111 in all, including the five declared earlier.
Tidal portA port where the water level depends on tides, requiring constant dredging — Deendayal Port and Kolkata are examples.
Riverine portAn inland port on a river — Shyama Prasad Mookerjee Port, Kolkata, serving the Ganga–Brahmaputra basin.
Hub portA central port that serves a whole region — Jawaharlal Nehru Port was planned to decongest Mumbai and act as a hub.
UDANUde Desh ka Aam Nagrik — the Regional Connectivity Scheme of the Ministry of Civil Aviation to make flying affordable and connect regional and remote routes.
First-class mailCards and envelopes, airlifted between stations by land and air.
Second-class mailBook packets, registered newspapers and periodicals, carried by surface mail over land and water.
Mass communicationRadio, television, newspapers, magazines, books and films, which provide entertainment and create awareness about national programmes and policies.
TradeThe exchange of goods among people, states and countries; the market is the place where such exchanges take place.
Balance of tradeThe difference between a country’s exports and imports; favourable when exports exceed imports, unfavourable when imports exceed exports.
Economic barometerA measure of a country’s economic prosperity — advancement of international trade is considered one.
PRASHADPilgrimage Rejuvenation and Spiritual Heritage Augmentation Drive — a scheme to boost tourism.

These are the “Can you…” and activity questions that appear inside the chapter text. Model answers are based on the chapter itself.

1.

Why is air travel preferred in the north-eastern states?

Model answer

Because the north-east has big rivers, dissected relief, dense forests, frequent floods and international frontiers. In the absence of air transport, access would be very difficult; air travel can cover difficult terrains with great ease and has made access easier. Pawanhans Helicopters Ltd. also provides services to inaccessible areas and difficult terrains.

2.

Which National Highway is the historical Sher Shah Suri Marg between Delhi and Amritsar known by?

Model answer

It is known as National Highway 1 (NH-1) in the older numbering. Under the new numbering it falls within NH-44. Check the current number on the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways website, as numbers have been revised.

3.

How can we help our railways run as per schedule?

Model answer

By buying tickets and never travelling without one; not pulling the chain unnecessarily or stopping trains; not damaging railway property or stealing fittings; keeping platforms and coaches clean; following safety rules at crossings; and reporting faults. Since thefts, ticketless travel and unnecessary chain-pulling cause heavy damage and delay, public cooperation is essential.

4.

Collect information on National Highway numbers (old and new).

Model answer

Old numbers (NH-1, NH-2 …) have been rationalised into new numbers (NH-44 is the longest, running north to south). The Ministry of Road Transport and Highways website lists both old and new numbers, state by state. (Student answers will vary.)

5.

Find out the current railway zones and their headquarters and locate them on the map.

Model answer

The Indian Railway is reorganised into 17 zones. The chapter does not list them, but the Southern Railway’s headquarters is Chennai (as asked in the Quiz Drive). Collect the full list from the Indian Railways website (indianrailways.gov.in) and mark the headquarters on an outline map. (Student answers will vary.)

6.

Railway line has been extended from Banihal to Baramula in the Kashmir Valley. Locate these two towns on the map of India.

Model answer

Banihal is in the Jammu region at the southern end of the Banihal pass, and Baramula lies in the Kashmir Valley to the north-west of Srinagar. The line runs through the valley from Banihal via Srinagar to Baramula.

7.

Prepare a project on heritage tourism in India, and show your state’s tourist places and their connectivity.

Model answer

Structure the project as: heritage sites of your state with a short description; how each is reached by rail, road and air; facilities available; problems faced by tourists; and suggestions for sustainable tourism. Mark the places on an outline map and draw the connecting rail, road and air routes. (Student project.)

8.

What type of tourism may be developed in your state and why? How can tourism help economic development sustainably?

Model answer

Answers vary by state — for example heritage tourism in Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh, eco tourism in the north-east and Kerala, adventure tourism in Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand, medical tourism in metro cities and pilgrimage tourism across the country. Tourism helps by generating local employment, supporting handicrafts and cultural pursuits, promoting national integration and bringing foreign exchange, provided it is planned so that the environment and local culture are not damaged. (Student answers will vary.)

08

NCERT Exercise Questions and Answers

End-of-chapter exercises, projects and activities

NCERT Exercises

Reproduced from the exercise section of the chapter, with model answers. Word limits are the ones the textbook sets.

1.
NCERT exercise1 mark

Multiple choice — Which two of the following extreme locations are connected by the east–west corridor? (a) Mumbai and Nagpur (b) Silchar and Porbandar (c) Mumbai and Kolkata (d) Nagpur and Siligudi

Model answer

(b) Silchar and Porbandar. The East–West corridor connects Silchar (Assam) and Porbandar (Gujarat); the North–South corridor links Srinagar and Kanniyakumari.

2.
NCERT exercise1 mark

Multiple choice — Which mode of transportation reduces trans-shipment losses and delays? (a) Railways (b) Roadways (c) Pipeline (d) Waterways

Model answer

(c) Pipeline. Pipelines rule out trans-shipment losses or delays, and their running costs are minimal.

3.
NCERT exercise1 mark

Multiple choice — Which one of the following states is not connected with the H.V.J. pipeline? (a) Madhya Pradesh (b) Maharashtra (c) Gujarat (d) Uttar Pradesh

Model answer

(b) Maharashtra. The Hazira–Vijaipur–Jagdishpur pipeline links Gujarat (Hazira), Madhya Pradesh (Vijaipur) and Uttar Pradesh (Jagdishpur).

4.
NCERT exercise1 mark

Multiple choice — Which one of the following ports is the deepest land-locked and well-protected port along the east coast? (a) Chennai (b) Paradwip (c) V.O. Chidambaranar (Tuticorin) (d) Vishakhapatnam

Model answer

(d) Vishakhapatnam. It was originally conceived as an outlet for iron ore exports.

5.
NCERT exercise1 mark

Multiple choice — Which one of the following is the most important mode of transportation in India? (a) Pipeline (b) Railways (c) Roadways (d) Airways

Model answer

(b) Railways. Railways are the principal mode of transportation for freight and passengers, and today they are more important in our national economy than all other means of transport put together.

6.
NCERT exercise1 mark

Multiple choice — Which one of the following terms is used to describe trade between two or more countries? (a) Internal trade (b) International trade (c) External trade (d) Local trade

Model answer

(b) International trade. The chapter defines trade between two countries as international trade, which may take place through sea, air or land routes.

7.
NCERT exercise3 marks

State any three merits of roadways. (about 30 words)

Model answer

Construction cost of roads is much lower than that of railway lines; roads can traverse dissected and undulating topography and negotiate higher gradients, even in the Himalayas; and they provide door-to-door service, lowering loading and unloading costs. They also act as feeders to other modes.

8.
NCERT exercise3 marks

Where and why is rail transport the most convenient means of transportation? (about 30 words)

Model answer

In the northern plains, with their vast level land, high population density and rich agricultural resources — the most favourable conditions for the growth of railways. Railways are the principal mode for freight and passengers over long distances.

9.
NCERT exercise3 marks

What is the significance of the border roads? (about 30 words)

Model answer

Built and maintained by the Border Roads Organisation (established 1960) in the northern and north-eastern border areas, they are of strategic importance, have improved accessibility in areas of difficult terrain and helped the economic development of these areas.

10.
NCERT exercise3 marks

What is meant by trade? What is the difference between international and local trade? (about 30 words)

Model answer

Trade is the exchange of goods among people, states and countries, carried out in markets. Local trade takes place within cities, towns and villages; international trade takes place between two countries, by sea, air or land routes.

11.
NCERT exercise5 marks

Why are the means of transportation and communication called the lifelines of a nation and its economy? (about 120 words)

Model answer

Because goods and services do not move from supply locales to demand locales on their own; transport moves them, and traders make them reach consumers. The pace of development of a country therefore depends on the production of goods and services as well as their movement over space, so efficient means of transport are prerequisites for fast development. Transport needs an equally developed communication system, and transport, communication and trade are complementary to each other. Railways, airways, waterways, newspapers, radio, television, cinema and the internet have contributed to India’s socio-economic progress in many ways, and trade from local to international levels has added to the vitality of its economy. A dense and efficient network of transport and communication is a prerequisite for local, national and global trade — which is why they are called the lifelines of the nation and its economy.

12.
NCERT exercise5 marks

Write a note on the changing nature of international trade in the last fifteen years. (about 120 words)

Model answer

International trade has expanded and changed in composition. India now has trade relations with all major trading blocks and all geographical regions of the world. Exports include gems and jewellery, chemicals and related products, and agriculture and allied products, while imports include petroleum crude and products, gems and jewellery, chemicals, base metals, electronic items, machinery, and agriculture and allied products. Two changes stand out: first, India has emerged as a software giant and earns large foreign exchange from exporting information technology, so services have become a major export; second, the growing demand for petroleum and electronic goods keeps the import bill high, making the balance of trade a matter of constant attention. Advancement of international trade remains the economic barometer of the country’s prosperity.

09

Important Questions and Answers

Board-style practice

Practice questions

Written in the style of CBSE board papers. They are additional practice, not NCERT originals.

1.

Why do roads have an edge over railways in India? (5 marks)

Model answer

(i) Construction cost of roads is much lower than that of railway lines. (ii) Roads can traverse comparatively more dissected and undulating topography. (iii) Roads can negotiate higher gradients of slopes and so can traverse mountains such as the Himalayas. (iv) Road transport is economical for transporting few persons and relatively smaller amounts of goods over short distances. (v) It provides door-to-door service, so loading and unloading costs are much lower. (vi) Road transport acts as a feeder to other modes, linking railway stations, air and sea ports. India has the second largest road network in the world, about 62.16 lakh km (2020–21).

2.

Describe the six classes of roads in India. (5 marks)

Model answer

Golden Quadrilateral Super Highways — Delhi–Kolkata–Chennai–Mumbai–Delhi by six-lane super highways, with the North–South corridor (Srinagar to Kanniyakumari) and East–West corridor (Silchar to Porbandar), implemented by NHAI to reduce time and distance between mega cities. National Highways — primary road systems linking extreme parts of the country, running largely north–south and east–west. State Highways — linking a state capital with district headquarters. District Roads — connecting district headquarters with other places in the district. Other Roads — rural roads linking villages with towns, given special impetus by the Pradhan Mantri Grameen Sadak Yojana. Border Roads — built and maintained by the Border Roads Organisation, established in 1960, for strategic roads in the northern and north-eastern border areas.

3.

What is the Golden Quadrilateral? What is its objective? (3 marks)

Model answer

A major road development project linking Delhi–Kolkata–Chennai–Mumbai–Delhi by six-lane super highways. The North–South corridor linking Srinagar and Kanniyakumari, and the East–West corridor connecting Silchar and Porbandar, are part of this project. Its major objective is to reduce the time and distance between the mega cities of India, and it is being implemented by the National Highway Authority of India.

4.

Describe the distribution of railways in India and the factors that influence it. (5 marks)

Model answer

The distribution pattern has been largely influenced by physiographic, economic and administrative factors. The northern plains, with vast level land, high population density and rich agricultural resources, provided the most favourable conditions, though many wide rivers required bridges. In the hilly terrains of the peninsular region, tracks are laid through low hills, gaps or tunnels, and the contiguous stretch of the Sahyadri could be crossed only through gaps or passes. The Himalayan mountainous regions are unfavourable because of high relief, sparse population and lack of economic opportunities. It was difficult to lay lines on the sandy plain of western Rajasthan, the swamps of Gujarat and the forested tracks of Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Odisha and Jharkhand. The Konkan Railway along the west coast has since facilitated movement in this important economic region, though it faces problems of sinking track and landslides.

5.

Describe the railway gauges of India with figures. (3 marks)

Model answer

The Indian Railway network runs on multiple gauge operations extending over 67,956 km: broad gauge (1.676 m) 63,950 km, metre gauge (1.000 m) 2,402 km and narrow gauge (0.762 and 0.610 m) 1,604 km.

6.

What are the problems faced by Indian Railways? (3 marks)

Model answer

Many passengers travel without tickets; thefts and damaging of railway property have not stopped completely; and people stop trains and pull the chain unnecessarily, causing heavy damage. The Konkan Railway also faces sinking of track in some stretches and landslides.

7.

Why are pipelines important? Name the three networks. (5 marks)

Model answer

Pipelines carry crude oil, petroleum products and natural gas from fields to refineries, fertiliser factories and thermal power plants, and solids when converted to slurry. The far inland locations of refineries like Barauni, Mathura and Panipat and gas-based fertiliser plants could be thought of only because of pipelines. Initial cost of laying is high but running costs are minimal, and pipelines rule out trans-shipment losses or delays. The three networks are: upper Assam oil fields to Kanpur via Guwahati, Barauni and Prayagraj; Salaya (Gujarat) to Jalandhar (Punjab) via Viramgam, Mathura, Delhi and Sonipat; and the 1,700 km Hazira–Vijaipur–Jagdishpur gas pipeline, with the gas pipeline network now 18,500 km.

8.

Why are waterways the cheapest means of transport? Describe the national waterways. (5 marks)

Model answer

Waterways are the cheapest means of transport, most suitable for carrying heavy and bulky goods, and fuel-efficient and environment-friendly. India has inland navigation waterways of 14,500 km, and 111 inland waterways were declared National Waterways by the National Waterways Act, 2016. The five described are N.W. No. 1 — the Ganga between Prayagraj and Haldia (1,620 km); N.W. No. 2 — the Brahmaputra between Sadiya and Dhubri (891 km); N.W. No. 3 — the West-Coast Canal in Kerala (205 km); N.W. No. 4 — stretches of the Godavari and Krishna with the Kakinada–Puducherry canals (1,078 km); and N.W. No. 5 — the Brahmani with the Matai, Mahanadi delta channels and East Coast Canal (588 km). Other waterways with substantial traffic are the Mandavi, Zuari and Cumberjua, Sunderbans, Barak and the backwaters of Kerala.

9.

Describe any five major ports of India with their special features. (5 marks)

Model answer

Deendayal Port (Kandla) — the first port developed after Independence, to ease trade on Mumbai port after the loss of Karachi; a tidal port serving the granary and industrial belt of J&K, Himachal Pradesh, Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan and Gujarat. Mumbai — the biggest port with a spacious natural, well-sheltered harbour. Jawaharlal Nehru Port — planned to decongest Mumbai and act as a hub port. Mormugao (Goa) — the premier iron ore exporting port, about fifty per cent of India’s iron ore export. New Mangalore — exports iron ore concentrates from Kudremukh. Vishakhapatnam — the deepest landlocked and well-protected port, conceived as an outlet for iron ore. Chennai — one of the oldest artificial ports, next to Mumbai in trade volume. Kolkata (Shyama Prasad Mookerjee) — an inland riverine port, tidal, requiring constant dredging of the Hoogly, with Haldia developed as its subsidiary.

10.

What is UDAN? (3 marks)

Model answer

UDAN (Ude Desh ka Aam Nagrik) is a first-of-its-kind scheme globally, designed to jump-start the regional aviation market. The Regional Connectivity Scheme (RCS)–UDAN was conceived by the Ministry of Civil Aviation to promote regional connectivity by making flying affordable for the common citizen, encouraging airlines to operate on regional and remote routes through enabling policies and incentives.

11.

Describe India’s postal and telecom network. (5 marks)

Model answer

The Indian postal network is the largest in the world and handles parcels as well as personal written communications. Cards and envelopes are first-class mail and are airlifted between stations by land and air; book packets, registered newspapers and periodicals are second-class mail carried by surface mail over land and water. Six mail channels — Rajdhani, Metro, Green, Business, Bulk Mail and Periodical — have been introduced for quick delivery in large towns. India has one of the largest telecom networks in Asia; excluding urban places, more than two-thirds of villages have STD facility, and the government has extended twenty-four-hour STD to every village at a uniform rate, made possible by integrating space technology with communication technology.

12.

Explain the balance of trade. (3 marks)

Model answer

Export and import are the components of trade. The balance of trade is the difference between a country’s exports and imports. When the value of exports exceeds the value of imports it is a favourable balance of trade; when imports exceed exports it is an unfavourable balance of trade. Advancement of international trade is an index of a country’s economic prosperity and is therefore called its economic barometer.

13.

Why is tourism important for India? (3 marks)

Model answer

Tourism has grown remarkably over two decades with government initiatives, infrastructure development and global branding. It promotes national integration, supports local handicrafts and cultural pursuits, and develops international understanding about our culture and heritage. Foreign tourists come for heritage, eco, adventure, cultural, medical and business tourism, and schemes like Swadesh Darshan 2.0, the Vibrant Village Programme, PRASHAD and Paryatan Mitra have been started to boost it.

Previous Year Questions (PYQs)

Asked in CBSE board exams

Previous year questions

These follow the pattern of questions set in CBSE Social Science papers for this chapter. Answers are model answers.

1.
CBSE pattern

Why is the Indian Railway called the largest public sector undertaking? (CBSE pattern, 2 marks)

Model answer

Because it is the largest public sector undertaking in the country, the principal mode of transportation for freight and passengers, reorganised into 17 zones and running over 67,956 km of track.

2.
CBSE pattern

Mention any two problems of Indian Railways. (2 marks)

Model answer

Many passengers travel without tickets; and theft and damaging of railway property, stopping trains and pulling the chain unnecessarily cause heavy damage and delay.

3.
CBSE pattern

What is a tidal port? Name two tidal ports of India. (2 marks)

Model answer

A port whose working depends on the tide and which therefore needs constant dredging. Deendayal Port (Kandla) and Shyama Prasad Mookerjee Port, Kolkata, are described as tidal ports in the chapter.

4.
CBSE pattern

Name the port that handles about fifty per cent of India’s iron ore export. (1 mark)

Model answer

Mormugao port in Goa — the premier iron ore exporting port of the country.

5.
CBSE pattern

Which is the world’s longest highway tunnel and who built it? (2 marks)

Model answer

The Atal Tunnel, 9.02 km long, built by the Border Roads Organisation; it connects Manali to the Lahul-Spiti valley throughout the year, in the Pir Panjal range at 3,000 m.

6.
CBSE pattern

Why are pipelines preferred for transporting liquids and gases? (3 marks)

Model answer

Because their running costs are minimal, they rule out trans-shipment losses or delays, and they make it possible to locate refineries and gas-based fertiliser plants far inland — as with Barauni, Mathura, Panipat and Jagdishpur. The initial cost of laying pipelines is high, but the advantages outweigh it.

7.
CBSE pattern

What are first-class and second-class mail? (2 marks)

Model answer

Cards and envelopes are first-class mail and are airlifted between stations covering both land and air. Book packets, registered newspapers and periodicals are second-class mail, carried by surface mail over land and water.

8.
CBSE pattern

Name the six mail channels introduced for quick delivery of mail. (2 marks)

Model answer

Rajdhani Channel, Metro Channel, Green Channel, Business Channel, Bulk Mail Channel and Periodical Channel.

9.
CBSE pattern

Which state is not connected by the HVJ pipeline and why? (2 marks)

Model answer

Maharashtra is not connected — the pipeline runs from Hazira (Gujarat) via Vijaipur (Madhya Pradesh) to Jagdishpur (Uttar Pradesh), linking the Mumbai High and Bassein gas fields with fertiliser, power and industrial complexes in western and northern India.

10.
CBSE pattern

What is meant by an unfavourable balance of trade? (2 marks)

Model answer

When the value of a country’s imports exceeds the value of its exports, the balance of trade is unfavourable. India’s imports of petroleum crude and products, electronic items and machinery contribute to this.

Frequently Asked Questions

Quick clarifications

1.

Which is the cheapest means of transport?

Model answer

Waterways — most suitable for heavy and bulky goods, and fuel-efficient and environment-friendly.

2.

Which mode is the fastest and most comfortable?

Model answer

Air travel — the fastest, most comfortable and most prestigious mode of transport.

3.

Which is the deepest landlocked port of India?

Model answer

Vishakhapatnam, which is also well protected and was conceived as an outlet for iron ore exports.

4.

Why does Kolkata port need dredging?

Model answer

Because it is a tidal riverine port on the Hoogly, so constant dredging is required to keep it navigable.

5.

What is a hub port?

Model answer

A port that serves a whole region and relieves pressure on another port — Jawaharlal Nehru Port was planned to decongest Mumbai and act as a hub for the region.

6.

How many railway zones are there?

Model answer

Seventeen — the Indian Railway has been reorganised into 17 zones.

7.

What is the difference between metalled and unmetalled roads?

Model answer

Metalled roads are made of cement, concrete or bitumen of coal and are all-weather roads; unmetalled roads go out of use in the rainy season.

8.

What does the Digital India programme aim at?

Model answer

To prepare India for a knowledge-based transformation, with the focus on being transformative — IT (Indian Talent) + IT (Information Technology) = IT (India Tomorrow) — and on making technology central to enabling change.

Assertion-Reason Questions

Choose the correct option

How to answer

(a) Both A and R are true and R explains A. (b) Both are true but R does not explain A. (c) A is true, R is false. (d) A is false, R is true.

1.

Assertion (A): Transport, communication and trade are complementary to each other.
Reason (R): Transport needs an equally developed communication system, and both serve trade.

2.

Assertion (A): Roadways have an edge over railways in India.
Reason (R): Construction cost of roads is much lower than that of railway lines.

3.

Assertion (A): The Atal Tunnel is the world’s longest highway tunnel.
Reason (R): It was built by the Border Roads Organisation in the Pir Panjal range.

4.

Assertion (A): The Himalayan region is favourable for railway construction.
Reason (R): The northern plains have vast level land and high population density.

5.

Assertion (A): Pipelines rule out trans-shipment losses and delays.
Reason (R): Their initial cost of laying is high but subsequent running costs are minimal.

6.

Assertion (A): Waterways are the cheapest means of transport.
Reason (R): They are most suitable for carrying heavy and bulky goods and are fuel-efficient.

7.

Assertion (A): Deendayal Port was developed soon after Independence.
Reason (R): Karachi port was lost to Pakistan after Partition.

8.

Assertion (A): Air travel is preferred in the north-eastern states.
Reason (R): The north-east has dissected relief, dense forests, frequent floods and international frontiers.

9.

Assertion (A): The Indian postal network is the smallest in the world.
Reason (R): It handles parcels as well as personal written communications.

10.

Assertion (A): Advancement of international trade is an index of economic prosperity.
Reason (R): No country can survive without international trade because resources are space bound.

Source-Based and Case-Based Questions

Read the passage or table, then answer

Source 1 — Why roads beat railways

Source extract

The growing importance of road transport vis-à-vis rail transport is rooted in the following reasons: (a) construction cost of roads is much lower than that of railway lines, (b) roads can traverse comparatively more dissected and undulating topography, (c) roads can negotiate higher gradients of slopes and as such can traverse mountains such as the Himalayas, (d) road transport is economical in transportation of few persons and relatively smaller amount of goods over short distances, (e) it also provides door-to-door service, thus the cost of loading and unloading is much lower, (f) road transport is also used as a feeder to other modes of transport such as they provide a link between railway stations, air and sea ports.

1.

Which two reasons are about terrain?

Model answer

(b) roads can traverse dissected and undulating topography, and (c) roads can negotiate higher gradients of slopes, even in the Himalayas.

2.

Which reason explains why a short trip with a small load is cheaper by road?

Model answer

Reason (d): road transport is economical for few persons and relatively smaller amounts of goods over short distances — helped by (e) door-to-door service, which lowers loading and unloading costs.

3.

What role do roads play for railways, ports and airports?

Model answer

They act as feeders, providing links between railway stations, air and sea ports.

Source 2 — Table 7.1: India’s railway track

Data interpretation
India: Railway Track (Railway Yearbook 2019–20)
Gauge in metresRoute (km)
Broad Gauge (1.676)63,950
Metre Gauge (1.000)2,402
Narrow Gauge (0.762 and 0.610)1,604
Total67,956

How to read this table: the gauge is the distance between the rails; the rows add up to the total route length.

1.

Which gauge dominates India’s railway network?

Model answer

Broad gauge, with 63,950 km of the 67,956 km total — about 94 per cent.

2.

What does “multiple gauge operations” mean?

Model answer

That the network runs on three different track widths — broad, metre and narrow gauge — so trains and track must be managed accordingly.

3.

Approximately how much of the network is narrow gauge?

Model answer

About 1,604 km, roughly 2.4 per cent of the total.

Source 3 — UDAN and regional connectivity

Case study

UDAN (Ude Desh ka Aam Nagrik) is a first-of-its-kind scheme globally, designed to jump-start the regional aviation market. Regional Connectivity Scheme (RCS)–UDAN was conceived by the Ministry of Civil Aviation (MoCA), Government of India, to promote regional connectivity by making flying affordable for the common citizen. The central idea of the scheme is to encourage airlines to operate flights on regional and remote routes through enabling policies and extending incentives.

1.

What does the acronym UDAN stand for?

Model answer

Ude Desh ka Aam Nagrik.

2.

How does the scheme try to increase regional flights?

Model answer

Through enabling policies and extending incentives that encourage airlines to operate on regional and remote routes.

3.

Which parts of India would benefit most from such a scheme, and why?

Model answer

The north-eastern states and other remote or difficult terrain areas — big rivers, dissected relief, dense forests, frequent floods and international frontiers make surface access difficult, so affordable air travel connects them.

On an outline map of India, mark the Golden Quadrilateral and the two corridors.

Delhi–Kolkata–Chennai–Mumbai–Delhi; North–South corridor Srinagar to Kanniyakumari; East–West corridor Silchar to Porbandar.

2.

Mark the twelve major ports of India.

Model answer

Use Map 7.2: Kandla (Deendayal), Mumbai, Jawaharlal Nehru, Mormugao, New Mangalore, Cochin, Tuticorin (V.O. Chidambaranar), Chennai, Vishakhapatnam, Paradwip, Kolkata (Shyama Prasad Mookerjee) and Haldia.

3.

Locate the five National Waterways.

Model answer

NW-1 Ganga (Prayagraj–Haldia); NW-2 Brahmaputra (Sadiya–Dhubri); NW-3 West-Coast Canal, Kerala; NW-4 Godavari–Krishna and Kakinada–Puducherry canals; NW-5 Brahmani–Matai–Mahanadi and East Coast Canal.

4.

Mark the headquarters of the Southern Railway and one other zone.

Model answer

Southern Railway — Chennai. Others include Mumbai (Central and Western), Kolkata (Eastern), Delhi, Guwahati, Secunderabad and Jabalpur.

5.

Locate Banihal and Baramula and explain their importance.

Model answer

They are the two ends of the extended railway line in the Kashmir Valley — Banihal at the southern end and Baramula in the north-west of the valley.

6.

Mark the Atal Tunnel and state what it connects.

Model answer

In the Pir Panjal range of the Himalayas at 3,000 m; it connects Manali to the Lahul-Spiti valley throughout the year.

17

HOTS and Competency-Based Questions

Think beyond the text

Higher order thinking

These ask you to apply, compare or evaluate. Model answers are indicative — your own well-reasoned answer can differ.

1.

A district has a new airport under UDAN but no all-weather road. Which investment should come first, and why?

Model answer

The road, in most cases: roads provide door-to-door service and act as feeders to airports and railway stations, so without them the airport cannot be reached. Roads are also cheaper to build and can negotiate difficult terrain. The airport adds value only once the last-mile link exists — which is exactly why road transport is called a feeder to other modes. (Model answer.)

2.

“Railways bind the economic life of the country.” Justify with examples from the chapter.

Model answer

Railways are the principal mode for freight and passengers, make business, sightseeing and pilgrimage possible, and over more than 150 years have been a great integrating force. They accelerate the development of industry and agriculture by moving bulky goods over long distances, and the network’s distribution follows economic logic — dense in the northern plains with rich agriculture and population, sparse in the Himalayas where there is little economic activity. The Konkan Railway has opened up a major economic region on the west coast. (Model answer.)

3.

Why does India need both pipelines and railways if both carry bulk material?

Model answer

Because they carry different things. Pipelines carry fluids — crude oil, petroleum products, natural gas — and solids only as slurry, continuously and without trans-shipment losses, which allows refineries at Barauni, Mathura and Panipat to exist far inland. Railways carry solids — grain, coal, ore, containers, people — in any quantity and to any destination on the network. Together they reduce the load on each other, and pipelines free rail capacity for other goods. (Model answer.)

4.

Compare a tidal port with a landlocked deep port. What does each need to function well?

Model answer

A tidal port such as Kolkata or Kandla depends on the tide, so it needs constant dredging to stay navigable. A deep, landlocked, well-protected port such as Vishakhapatnam has natural depth and shelter but needs rail and road links to its hinterland. Both need efficient hinterland transport, warehousing and customs facilities; the tidal port additionally needs continuous dredging investment. (Model answer.)

5.

Tourism is called a trade. What does India export when a foreign tourist visits, and what risks must be managed?

Model answer

India exports services — accommodation, transport, guiding, food, handicrafts and cultural experiences — earning foreign exchange without shipping goods abroad. Tourism promotes national integration and supports local handicrafts. The risks are environmental damage, overcrowding at heritage sites, pressure on water and waste systems, and commercialisation of local culture; hence schemes such as Swadesh Darshan 2.0 and the emphasis on sustainable development. (Model answer.)

6.

“Communication is as important as transport.” Defend this statement using the chapter.

Model answer

Because transport without communication cannot be organised: goods must be ordered, tracked and paid for, and news of demand must travel faster than the goods. The chapter says transport has converted the world into a large village only with the help of an equally developed communication system, and that transport, communication and trade are complementary. India’s postal network, telecom network, All India Radio, Doordarshan, newspapers in about 100 languages and the Digital India programme all strengthen the flow of information from the grassroot upwards. (Model answer.)

Quick Revision Sheet

One page before the exam

Why lifelines

  • Goods and services do not move themselves; traders move them.
  • Pace of development depends on production and movement over space.
  • Land, water and air transport; transport + communication + trade are complementary.

Roadways

  • Second largest network, 62.16 lakh km (2020–21); six reasons roads beat rail.
  • Six classes: Golden Quadrilateral (+ N–S and E–W corridors, NHAI), National, State, District, Other (PMGSY), Border (BRO, 1960).
  • Metalled = all weather; unmetalled unusable in rain. Atal Tunnel 9.02 km, Pir Panjal, 3,000 m.

Railways

  • Principal mode; largest PSO; 17 zones; 1853 Mumbai–Thane, 34 km.
  • Distribution: physiography, economy, administration. Problems: ticketless travel, theft, chain pulling.
  • Gauges: BG 63,950; MG 2,402; NG 1,604; total 67,956 km. Konkan Railway on the west coast.

Pipelines

  • Crude oil, products, gas; solids as slurry; high initial cost, low running cost, no trans-shipment losses.
  • Three networks: Assam–Kanpur; Salaya–Jalandhar; HVJ 1,700 km → 18,500 km.

Waterways and ports

  • Cheapest, fuel-efficient, environment-friendly; 14,500 km inland; 111 NWs (2016 Act).
  • NW1 Ganga 1,620; NW2 Brahmaputra 891; NW3 Kerala 205; NW4 Godavari–Krishna 1,078; NW5 Brahmani–Mahanadi 588.
  • Coast 11,098.81 km; 12 major + 200 non-major; 95% volume, 68% value by sea.
  • Kandla first after Independence; Mumbai biggest; JNPT hub; Mormugao 50% iron ore; New Mangalore (Kudremukh); Cochin; Tuticorin; Chennai oldest artificial; Vishakhapatnam deepest; Paradwip iron ore; Kolkata riverine; Haldia subsidiary.

Airways and communication

  • Fastest, most comfortable; Pawanhans helicopters; UDAN.
  • Postal network largest in the world; first-class (cards, envelopes) and second-class mail; six mail channels.
  • Telecom among largest in Asia; two-thirds of villages with STD; 24-hour STD.
  • AIR, Doordarshan, newspapers in ~100 languages (most in Hindi), largest producer of feature films, CBFC, Digital India.

Trade and tourism

  • Trade = exchange of goods; international trade between countries; economic barometer.
  • Balance of trade: favourable if exports > imports, unfavourable if imports > exports.
  • Exports: gems and jewellery, chemicals, agriculture products. Imports: petroleum crude and products, gems, chemicals, base metals, electronics, machinery.
  • Tourism: Swadesh Darshan 2.0, Vibrant Village Programme, PRASHAD, Paryatan Mitra; heritage, eco, adventure, cultural, medical, business tourism.

Chapter Summary

The whole chapter in a few paragraphs

Goods and services do not move from supply to demand locations on their own, so transport is essential; traders make products reach consumers, and the pace of development depends on production as well as movement over space. Transport is classified into land, water and air, and it needs an equally developed communication system — transport, communication and trade are complementary and together are the lifelines of the nation and its economy.

India has the second largest road network in the world, about 62.16 lakh km (2020–21), with six classes of roads: Golden Quadrilateral super highways with the North–South and East–West corridors under NHAI, National Highways, State Highways, District Roads, Other Roads under the Pradhan Mantri Grameen Sadak Yojana, and Border Roads under the Border Roads Organisation (1960). Railways, the largest public sector undertaking, run 17 zones over 67,956 km of track on broad, metre and narrow gauges, from the first Mumbai–Thane line of 1853; pipelines carry oil, petroleum products and gas with minimal running cost and no trans-shipment losses; waterways, the cheapest mode, include five important national waterways; and twelve major ports handle 95 per cent of India’s foreign trade by volume.

Air travel is the fastest and most comfortable mode and is vital in the north-east, supported by UDAN. Communication — the world’s largest postal network, one of Asia’s largest telecom networks, All India Radio, Doordarshan, newspapers in about a hundred languages, the largest feature film industry and Digital India — completes the network.

International trade, whose advancement is the economic barometer of a country, consists of exports and imports, and the difference between them is the balance of trade. Tourism, promoted through Swadesh Darshan 2.0, the Vibrant Village Programme, PRASHAD and Paryatan Mitra, promotes national integration, supports handicrafts and culture, and earns foreign exchange.
